A linguist is a person who works with language at a deep, expert level. But here is the important thing to know right away: this word has two distinct meanings, and people use them in different situations. Knowing both will save you from confusion for the rest of your life.

This is the precise, correct meaning in formal and academic contexts.

A linguist is a person who scientifically studies language itself — how it is structured, how it works, how it changes over time, and how humans use it. This person is essentially a scientist, but their subject of research is language.

Crucially, a linguist in this sense is not necessarily someone who speaks many languages. They study language as a human phenomenon, not necessarily many individual languages. A linguist could spend their entire career studying only English and still be a brilliant linguist.

What exactly does such a linguist study?

Language is an enormous subject, so linguists tend to specialize in one or more areas:

  • Sounds — How are the sounds of a language produced? How do they combine? (e.g., Why does "ng" never start a word in English?)
  • Words — How are words built and formed? How do prefixes and suffixes work?
  • Sentences — What rules determine whether a sentence is grammatically correct or not? Why does "She gave him a book" sound fine, but "She donated him a book" sound wrong?
  • Meaning — How do words and sentences carry meaning? How does context change what something means?
  • Language in society — How does someone's social background, region, or class affect the way they speak? Why do accents exist?
  • Language in the mind — How do babies acquire language? What happens in the brain when we speak or understand speech?
  • Language over time — How and why do languages change across centuries? How did modern English grow out of older forms?
  • Languages in relation to each other — How are different languages related? What do all human languages have in common?

A person who studies any one (or more) of these areas professionally is a linguist.

In casual, everyday conversation, people often use "linguist" to mean a person who speaks several languages fluently. If someone says, "She's a remarkable linguist — she speaks French, Mandarin, Arabic, and Portuguese," they are using the word in this informal sense.

This usage is extremely common and widely understood, so it is not "wrong" in everyday speech. However, it is imprecise, and in academic or professional circles, it can cause confusion.
The Key Distinction You Must Know

This is the most important nuance of this word, and most people miss it:

Academic LinguistInformal "Linguist"

An academic linguist studies how language works as a system. They are researchers and scholars. A person who merely speaks many languages is more accurately called a polyglot — and these are two very different things.

Think of it this way: a music theorist studies how music works — its structure, harmony, and patterns. They may not be a great performer at all. Similarly, a linguist studies how language works. They may not speak many languages themselves.

Conversely, a brilliant concert pianist who can play 10 instruments is not automatically a music theorist. Similarly, someone who speaks 8 languages fluently is not automatically a linguist — they are a polyglot.

Of course, some people are both — a linguist who also speaks many languages — but the two qualities are independent of each other.

Noam Chomsky is perhaps the most famous linguist in the world. He proposed the theory that humans are born with an in-built mental capacity for language — that our brains are "pre-wired" to learn grammar. His work changed how we understand the human mind. He is a linguist in the strictest, most powerful sense of the word. His fame comes not from how many languages he speaks, but from what he discovered about language itself.
One Closely Related Word to Know

Linguistics (noun) — This is the academic discipline or field of study that linguists work in. It is the scientific study of language. Just as a biologist practices biology, a linguist practices linguistics.

A linguist is, precisely, a scholar who scientifically studies language — its sounds, structure, meaning, history, and role in the mind and society. Informally and loosely, the word is also used to mean someone who speaks many languages fluently, though the more accurate word for that is polyglot. The distinction matters: speaking many languages and scientifically studying language are related but different skills.
